I am also grateful to Mark Behrens, Robert Burklund, Tyler Lawson, Lennart Meier, and Andrew Senger for helpful discussions, and in particular to Robert Burklund for providing helpful comments on a draft.

## 2. Background on Hodge theory

In this section, we recall some background on Hodge theory for cubic curves over a general base scheme. Multiple sources (such as [Kat73, Appendix A1.2]) discuss Hodge theory for (smooth) elliptic curves.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism of schemes. One then has the $f^{-1}\mathcal{O}_{Y}$ -linear relative de Rham complex $\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/Y}$ .

#### Definition 2.1.

The $i$ th relative de Rham cohomology $\mathrm{H}^{i}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/Y)$ of $f:X\to Y$ is defined to be the hypercohomology sheaf $\mathbf{R}^{i}f_{\ast}(\Omega^{\bullet}_{X/Y})$ on $Y$ .

The Tot spectral sequence defines the Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence of sheaves on $Y$ :

$$ E_{1}^{s,t}=R^{t}f_{\ast}\Omega^{s}_{X/Y}\Rightarrow\mathrm{H}^{s+t}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/Y). $$

The following (easy) result is well-known.

#### Theorem 2.2.

If $f:X\to Y$ is a smooth, proper, and surjective morphism of relative dimension $1$ with geometrically connected fibers, then the Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence degenerates at the $E_{1}$ -page.

Since $f$ is of relative dimension $1$ , the only interesting de Rham cohomology is in the middle dimension, i.e., $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/Y)$ . In particular, for such $f$ , there is an exact sequence

$$ 0\to f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{X/Y}\to\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/Y)\to R^{1}f_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{X}\to 0 $$

of quasicoherent sheaves on $Y$ ; this is called the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence. Moreover, the pairing $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/Y)\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{Y}}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/Y)\to\mathcal{O}_{Y}$ is determined by the canonical perfect pairing

$$ R^{1}f_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{X}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{Y}}f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{X/Y}\to R^{1}f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{X/Y}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{trace}}\mathcal{O}_{Y}. $$

We now specialize to the case when $f:X\to Y$ is an elliptic curve $f:E\to S$ . Then $f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{E/S}$ is the line bundle $\omega_{E/S}$ of invariant differentials. The pairing $\omega_{E/S}\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{S}}R^{1}f_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{E}\to\mathcal{O}_{S}$ is perfect, and so $R^{1}f_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{E}\cong\omega_{E/S}^{-1}$ . In particular, the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence for $E\to S$ becomes

$$ 0\to\omega_{E/S}\to\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(E/S)\to\omega_{E/S}^{-1}\to 0. $$

If ${M}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ denotes the moduli stack of elliptic curves, and $\mathcal{E}\to{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ is the universal elliptic curve, then (2) exhibits $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{ell}})$ as an element of $\Ext^{1}_{{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}}(\omega^{-1},\omega)$ .

#### Remark 2.3.

If $S$ is a $p$ -adic scheme, then (2) corresponds to the Hodge filtration of the Dieudonné module $\mathbf{D}(E[p^{\infty}]/S)$ of $E$ under the isomorphism $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(E/S)\cong\mathbf{D}(E[p^{\infty}]/S)$ ; see, for instance, [Kat81, Section V].

The following is an immediate consequence of [Kat73, Equation A1.2.3]:

#### Proposition 2.4.

If $f:E\to S$ is an elliptic curve, then there is an isomorphism $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(E/S)\otimes\omega_{E/S}\cong f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{E/S}(\infty)^{\otimes 2}$ .

The map

$$ f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{E/S}(\infty)^{\otimes 2}\cong\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(E/S)\otimes\omega_{E/S}\to\omega_{E/S}^{-1}\otimes\omega_{E/S}=\mathcal{O}_{S} $$

induced by the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence sends a section of $f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{E/S}(\infty)^{\otimes 2}$ to its residue at $\infty$ .

We can now generalize the above story to the non-smooth setting. First, we recall the definition of a cubic curve.

#### Definition 2.5.

A cubic curve $f:E\to S$ over a scheme $S$ is a flat and proper morphism of finite presentation whose fibers are reduced, irreducible curves of arithmetic genus $1$ , along with a section $\infty:S\to E$ whose image is contained in the smooth locus $E^{\mathrm{sm}}$ of $f$ . Let ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ denote the stack of cubic curves, and let $f:\mathcal{E}\to{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ denote the universal cubic curve.

Let $\omega$ denote the line bundle on ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ assigning to a cubic curve $f:E\to S$ the cotangent bundle $\omega_{E/S}$ along the section $\infty$ . The vector bundle $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{ell}})$ over ${M}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ extends to a vector bundle, denoted $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}})$ , over ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ ; this vector bundle is represented by an element in $\Ext^{1}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\omega^{-1},\omega)\cong\mathrm{H}^{1}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}};\omega^{\otimes 2})$ . Upon tensoring $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}})$ with $\omega$ , we obtain for every cubic curve $f:E\to S$ an exact sequence

$$ 0\to\omega_{E/S}^{\otimes 2}\to f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{E/S}(\infty)^{\otimes 2}\to f_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{E/S}\cong\mathcal{O}_{S}\to 0, $$

which we shall refer to as the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence.

#### Definition 2.6.

Let ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ denote the moduli stack of cubic curves with a chosen splitting of the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence, and let ${M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{dR}}={M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}\times_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}$ denote the moduli stack of elliptic curves with a chosen splitting of the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence.

In order to do calculations with ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ , we would like to obtain a Hopf algebroid presentation of this stack. To do so, we recall a Hopf algebroid presentation of ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ . Zariski-locally on any base scheme $S$ , a cubic curve is described by a Weierstrass equation

$$ y^{2}+a_{1}xy+a_{3}y=x^{3}+a_{2}x^{2}+a_{4}x+a_{6}, $$

with other choices of coordinates $(x,y)$ given by the transformations

$$ x\mapsto x+r,\ y\mapsto y+sx+t. $$

The moduli stack ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ of cubic curves is presented by the Hopf algebroid

$$ (D,\Gamma)=(\mathbf{Z}[a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4},a_{6}],D[r,s,t]), $$

with gradings $|a_{i}|=i$ and $|r|=2$ , $|s|=1$ , and $|t|=3$ . Studying how the coefficients $a_{i}$ transform gives the right unit $\eta_{R}:D\to\Gamma$ of this Hopf algebroid:

$$ \displaystyle a_{1} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{1}+2s, \displaystyle a_{2} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{2}-a_{1}s+3r-s^{2}, \displaystyle a_{3} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{3}+a_{1}r+2t, \displaystyle a_{4} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{4}+a_{3}s+2a_{2}r-a_{1}t-a_{1}rs-2st+3r^{2}, \displaystyle a_{6} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{6}+a_{4}r-a_{3}t+a_{2}r^{2}-a_{1}rt-t^{2}+r^{3}. $$

To determine a Hopf algebroid presentation of ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ , note that the coordinate $x$ defines a function on $\mathcal{E}$ with double pole at $\infty$ , and that it is in fact the only such non-constant function on the smooth locus of $\mathcal{E}$ (this follows from the usual calculation [KM85, Section 2.2.5] with the Riemann-Roch formula). In particular, Proposition 2.4 implies that the element $[r]$ in the cobar complex for the Hopf algebroid $(D,\Gamma)$ detects the extension in $\Ext^{1}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\mathcal{O},\omega^{\otimes 2})=\Ext^{1,2}_{\Gamma}(D,D)$ determined by the de Rham cohomology $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{ell}})$ . By the exact sequence (3), a choice of Hodge–de Rham splitting on the universal cubic curve amounts to fixing a choice of coordinate $x$ (although $y$ is allowed to vary). Consequently:

#### Proposition 2.7.

The moduli stack ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ of cubic curves with a chosen splitting of the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence is presented by the Hopf algebroid $(D,\Sigma)=(\mathbf{Z}[a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4},a_{6}],D[s,t])$ , with gradings11 1 Recall that the topological grading is double the algebraic grading. $|a_{i}|=i$ , $|s|=1$ , and $|t|=3$ . The right unit is the same as in that of the elliptic curve Hopf algebroid, except with $r=0$ :

$$ \displaystyle a_{1} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{1}+2s, \displaystyle a_{2} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{2}-a_{1}s-s^{2}, \displaystyle a_{3} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{3}+2t, \displaystyle a_{4} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{4}+a_{3}s-a_{1}t-2st, \displaystyle a_{6} \displaystyle\mapsto a_{6}-a_{3}t-t^{2}. $$

## 3. The relationship with $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$

In this section, we study the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -quotient $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ of $\mathrm{tmf}$ by $\nu$ , and relate its Adams–Novikov spectral sequence to the cohomology of ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ .

We begin by recalling one construction of the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -quotient $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . This satisfies the following universal property: if $R$ is any $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ - $\mathrm{tmf}$ -algebra, then

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathrm{tmf}))}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu,R)=\begin{cases}\Omega^{\infty+4}R&\text{if }\nu=0\in\pi_{3}R\\
\emptyset&\text{else}.\end{cases} $$

One of the main results of [AB19] justifies the following definition:

#### Definition 3.1.

The $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ , called topological quasimodular forms (see Remark 4.2 for a justification for the name), is the Thom spectrum of the dotted extension in the following diagram:

$$ \textstyle{S^{4}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\nu} \textstyle{B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathrm{tmf})} \textstyle{\Omega S^{5}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} $$

#### Remark 3.2.

The element $\nu\in\pi_{3}(\mathrm{tmf})$ is spherical, and so this diagram factors as

$$ \textstyle{S^{4}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{2v_{1}^{2}} \textstyle{\mathrm{BSpin}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{J} \textstyle{B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Omega S^{5}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathrm{tmf}).} $$

Following the notation of [Dev19], we will write $A$ to denote the Thom spectrum of the loop map $\Omega S^{5}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ . Then there is a canonical equivalence $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu\simeq\mathrm{tmf}\otimes A$ of $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ - $\mathrm{tmf}$ -algebras, so there is in particular a ring map $A\to\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ .

The $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring $A$ will be useful below. In [Dev19], it is shown that there is an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -map $A\to\mathrm{BP}$ . Moreover, the $\mathrm{BP}$ -homology of $A$ at the prime $2$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}[y_{2}]$ , where $y_{2}$ is sent to $t_{1}^{2}$ modulo decomposables under the map $\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(A)\to\mathrm{BP}_{\ast}(\mathrm{BP})$ . In particular, $\mathrm{H}_{\ast}(A;\mathbf{F}_{2})\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[\zeta_{1}^{4}]$ . One then has:

#### Proposition 3.3.

There is a nontrivial simple $2$ -torsion element $\sigma_{1}\in\langle\eta,\nu,1_{A}\rangle\subseteq\pi_{5}(A)\cong\pi_{5}(C\nu)$ specified up to indeterminacy by the relation $\eta\nu=0$ . One choice of this element is represented by $[t_{2}]$ in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $A$ , and by $h_{21}$ in the (mod $2$ ) Adams spectral sequence for $A$ .

To connect $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ and Hodge theory for cubic curves, we make the following observation. Recall that $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}})\in\Ext^{1}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\omega^{-1},\omega)$ .

#### Proposition 3.4.

Let $f:\mathcal{E}\to{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ denote the universal cubic curve over the moduli stack of cubic curves. Then $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}})\in\Ext^{1}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\omega^{-1},\omega)\cong\mathrm{H}^{1}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}};\omega^{2})$ detects $\nu$ in the $E_{2}$ -page of the descent spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}$ .

#### Proof.

This is essentially argued in [Hop02, Section 5.2]. We know that $\mathrm{H}^{1}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}};\omega^{2})=\mathbf{Z}/12$ by the calculations in [Bau08]; the element $[r]$ in the cobar complex determined by the Hopf algebroid $(D,\Gamma)$ is a representative for the generator. This element detects $\nu$ in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}$ , and by the discussion before Proposition 2.7, also detects the extension class of the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence. ∎

#### Corollary 3.5.

The rank two vector bundle $\mathcal{F}(C\nu)$ on the moduli stack of cubic curves corresponding to $C\nu$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}})$ .

#### Remark 3.6.

In [Rez13, Section 11.5], the Hodge–de Rham exact sequence appears in a different but related guise, as a class in the $E_{2}$ -page of a spectral sequence $\{E_{r}^{s,t}\}$ converging to the homotopy groups of the space of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -maps $\mathbf{Z}_{+}\to\mathrm{TMF}$ . The element $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{ell}})\in E_{2}^{1,4}$ detects a nontrivial class in $\pi_{3}\mathrm{Map}_{{\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}}(\mathbf{Z}_{+},\mathrm{TMF})=\pi_{3}\mathbb{G}_{m}(\mathrm{TMF})$ , i.e., an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $K(\mathbf{Z},3)_{+}\to\mathrm{TMF}$ . This is related to the ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -twisting of $\mathrm{TMF}$ explored in [ABG10].

Since $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ is the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -quotient of $\mathrm{tmf}$ by $\nu$ by Remark 3.2, it is the universal $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ - $\mathrm{tmf}$ -algebra with a nullhomotopy of $\nu$ . If $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ is a homotopy commutative ring (which we will show is indeed the case in Corollary 4.8), then we would be able to consider the stack associated to $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ (in the sense of [DFHH14, Chapter 9], [Mat16, Section 2.1]), and it would be reasonable to expect that Proposition 3.4 implies that this stack is the moduli of cubic curves with a choice of splitting of the Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence. We have:

#### Theorem 3.7.

Let $g:{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}\to{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ denote the structure morphism. Then the sheaf on ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ associated to $A$ is isomorphic as an algebra to the pushforward $g_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a presentable symmetric monoidal ( $\infty$ -)category, and let $T$ denote the functor $\mathcal{C}^{\mathrm{unital}}\to\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}(\mathcal{C})$ sending a unital object $i:\mathbf{1}\to X$ to the free $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -algebra in $\mathcal{C}$ whose unit factors through $i$ : this may be defined via the homotopy pushout

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{Free}_{\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}(\mathbf{1})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathbf{1}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{Free}_{\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}(X)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{T(X)} $$

in $\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}(\mathcal{C})$ . The functor $\mathcal{F}(-)$ from the homotopy category of $\mathrm{tmf}$ -modules to $\QCoh({M}_{\mathrm{cub}})$ fits into a commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{h\mathrm{Mod}(\mathrm{tmf})^{\mathrm{unital}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{T} \textstyle{h\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{{1}}}(\mathrm{Mod}(\mathrm{tmf}))\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{T} \textstyle{\QCoh({M}_{\mathrm{cub}})^{\mathrm{unital}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathrm{assoc}}(\QCoh({M}_{\mathrm{cub}})).} $$

It is easy to see by the universal property of $T$ that $T(C\nu)\simeq A$ , so it follows from Proposition 3.4 that $\mathcal{F}(A)\cong T(f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\infty)^{\otimes 2})$ . It therefore suffices to show that $T(f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\infty)^{\otimes 2})\cong g_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}}$ . This is not immediate, since the sheaf $T(f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\infty)^{\otimes 2})$ satisfies a universal property with respect to associative $\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}$ -algebras. Nonetheless, its universal property defines an algebra map $\varphi:T(f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\infty)^{\otimes 2})\to g_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}}$ of sheaves on ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}$ . To check that this is an isomorphism, it suffices to show by [Mat16, Lemma 4.4] that the map induces an isomorphism on the cuspidal cubic over $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ for all primes $p$ .

In fact, we can check this over $\mathbf{Z}$ . We know that $g_{\ast}\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}}$ is isomorphic to a polynomial ring on a single generator: indeed, the space of all splittings of the Hodge filtration is isomorphic to the projective line $\mathbf{P}(\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}))$ minus the point corresponding to the line determined by the invariant differentials. Moreover, $T(f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\infty)^{\otimes 2})$ is isomorphic to a free associative ring on one generator, which is also a polynomial ring on a single generator. It therefore suffices to show that the generator maps to the generator under the algebra map $\varphi$ , but this (after unwinding) is precisely the fact (Proposition 2.4) that $\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{dR}}(\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}})\otimes\omega=f_{\ast}\Omega^{1}_{\mathcal{E}/{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}(\infty)^{\otimes 2}$ . ∎

#### Corollary 3.8.

There is a descent spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{s,2t}=\mathrm{H}^{s}({{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes t})\Rightarrow\pi_{2t-s}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu), $$

and it is isomorphic to the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ .

#### Proof.

There is a descent spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{s,2t}=\mathrm{H}^{s}({{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}};\mathcal{F}(A)\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}}\omega^{\otimes t})\Rightarrow\pi_{2t-s}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu), $$

and this is isomorphic to the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ by [Mat16, Corollary 5.3] and the main theorem of [Dev18]. Combining Theorem 3.7 with the projection isomorphism shows that $\mathcal{F}(A)\otimes_{\mathcal{O}_{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}}}\omega^{\otimes t}\cong g_{\ast}(g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes t})$ . The morphism $g$ is flat and affine, so $E_{2}^{s,2t}\cong\mathrm{H}^{s}({{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes t})$ , as desired. ∎

#### Remark 3.9.

Corollary 3.8 says that although $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ is not a priori a homotopy commutative ring, there is a descent spectral sequence which would exist if there was a sheaf of structured ring spectra on ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ whose global sections was $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . We pose this as a conjecture:

#### Conjecture 3.10.

For some $k\geq 2$ , there is a sheaf of even-periodic $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ -rings $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{der}}$ on the étale site of ${M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ such that if $f:\spec R\to{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ is an étale map, then $\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{der}}(f)$ is the Landweber-exact theory corresponding to the composite $\spec R\to{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{dR}}\to{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}\to{M}_{FG}$ , and such that the global sections $\Gamma({M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{dR}};\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{der}})$ is equivalent as an $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring to $\mathrm{TMF}/\!\!/\nu$ . Moreover, the resulting $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ -ring structure on $\mathrm{TMF}/\!\!/\nu$ extends to an $\mathbf{E}_{{k}}$ -ring structure on $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ .

## 4. The descent spectral sequence

Our goal in this section is to calculate the homotopy groups of $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ via the descent spectral sequence of Corollary 3.8. To do this calculation, we will use the Hopf algebroid presentation in Proposition 2.7. The calculation of the descent spectral sequence was done independently by Charles Rezk; although he stated part of the result to us in an email, the argument is ours (so errors are our fault).

#### Theorem 4.1.

There is an isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{H}^{\ast}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes\ast})\cong\mathbf{Z}[b_{2},b_{4},b_{6},b_{8},h_{1},h_{21}]/I, $$

where $b_{i}\in\mathrm{H}^{0}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes i})$ of total degree $2i$ , $h_{1}\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega)$ of total degree $1$ , and $h_{21}\in\mathrm{H}^{1}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes 3})$ of total degree $5$ . If one defines

$$ \displaystyle c_{4} \displaystyle=b_{2}^{2}-24b_{4},\ c_{6}=-b_{2}^{3}+36b_{2}b_{4}-216b_{6}, \displaystyle\Delta \displaystyle=-b_{2}^{2}b_{8}-8b_{4}^{3}-27b_{6}^{2}+9b_{2}b_{4}b_{6}, $$

then the ideal $I$ is generated by the relations

$$ 2h_{1}=0,\ 2h_{21}=0,\ h_{1}^{2}b_{6}=h_{21}^{2}b_{2},\ 4b_{8}=b_{2}b_{6}-b_{4}^{2},\ 1728\Delta=c_{4}^{3}-c_{6}^{2}. $$

Moreover, the descent/Adams–Novikov spectral sequence of Corollary 3.8 collapses on the $E_{4}$ -page, and $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu)$ is determined by the differentials

$$ d_{3}(b_{2})=h_{1}^{3},\ d_{3}(b_{4})=h_{1}^{2}h_{21},\ d_{3}(b_{6})=h_{1}h_{21}^{2},\ d_{3}(b_{8})=h_{21}^{3}. $$

One has the relations

$$ \eta^{3}=0,\ \eta^{2}\sigma_{1}=0,\ \eta\sigma_{1}^{2}=0,\ \sigma_{1}^{3}=0 $$

in the homotopy of $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ , in addition to the relations in $I$ . Here $\eta$ is represented by $h_{1}$ , and $\sigma_{1}$ is represented by $h_{21}$ . All the torsion in $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ is concentrated in dimensions congruent to $1,2\pmod{4}$ .

Before giving the proof, we discuss some consequences.

#### Remark 4.2.

By Theorem 4.1, there is a ring isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{H}^{0}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes\ast})\cong\mathbf{Z}[b_{2},b_{4},b_{6},b_{8}]/(4b_{8}=b_{2}b_{6}-b_{4}^{2},\ 1728\Delta=c_{4}^{3}-c_{6}^{2}). $$

This ring has been studied before (in characteristic zero, in which case $b_{8}=(b_{2}b_{6}-b_{4}^{2})/4$ ), e.g., in [KZ95, Mov12], where it is referred to as the ring of quasimodular forms. Theorem 4.1 provides a calculation of the ring of integral quasimodular forms, and also justifies calling the ring spectrum $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ by the name “topological quasimodular forms”.

The following corollary is a calculation via Theorem 4.1.

#### Corollary 4.3.

In Adams–Novikov filtration zero, $b_{i}^{2}$ and twice any monomial in the $b_{i}$ s survive to the $E_{\infty}$ -page for $i=2,4,6,8$ , as do $b_{2}b_{6}$ and $\lambda_{1}b_{8}b_{2}^{2}+\lambda_{2}b_{2}b_{4}b_{6}$ for $\lambda_{1}\equiv\lambda_{2}\pmod{2}$ . In particular, $\Delta\in\pi_{24}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu)$ , so the $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring $\mathrm{TMF}/\!\!/\nu$ is $24$ -periodic with periodicity generator $\Delta$ .

#### Remark 4.4.

Note that $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ is complex orientable after inverting $2$ . This can be seen algebraically by noting that the Hopf algebroid $(D,\Sigma)$ presenting ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ becomes discrete after inverting $2$ ; indeed, the transformation $y\to y-a_{1}x/2-a_{3}/2$ transforms the Weierstrass equation (4) into

$$ y^{2}=x^{3}+a_{2}x^{2}+a_{4}x+a_{6}, $$

and one cannot make any coordinate changes to $x$ since it is fixed. We find that $(D,\Sigma)$ is isomorphic to the discrete Hopf algebroid $(D^{\prime}=\mathbf{Z}[1/2][a_{2},a_{4},a_{6}],D^{\prime})$ , and so $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{tmf}[1/2]/\!\!/\nu)\cong\mathbf{Z}[1/2][a_{2},a_{4},a_{6}]$ , with $|a_{i}|=2i$ . In light of this, we only need to prove Theorem 4.1 after $2$ -localization.

#### Remark 4.5.

The Hurewicz image of $\mathrm{tmf}$ in $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ can be determined from Theorem 4.1. The subring generated by $\eta$ , $\sigma_{1}$ , $2b_{2}$ , and $b_{2}^{2}$ is in the image of the map $\pi_{\ast}A\to\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . There relationship between $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu)$ and $\pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{tmf})$ , however, is more interesting than merely the Hurewicz image. The ( $2$ -local) calculation in [Bau08] shows that $\overline{\kappa}\nu$ vanishes in $\pi_{23}(\mathrm{tmf})$ ; this is detected in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence by a $d_{5}$ -differential $d_{5}(\Delta)=\overline{\kappa}\nu$ . This implies that the element $8\Delta\in\pi_{24}(\mathrm{tmf})$ can be expressed as an element of the Toda bracket $\langle 8,\nu,\overline{\kappa}\rangle$ . Equivalently, the map $\overline{\kappa}:S^{20}\to\mathrm{tmf}$ extends to a map from $\Sigma^{20}C\nu$ , and hence from $\Sigma^{20}\mathrm{tmf}\wedge C\nu$ . Composition with the map $S^{24}\to\Sigma^{20}C\nu$ which is degree $8$ on the top cell produces the element $8\Delta\in\pi_{24}\mathrm{tmf}$ (up to indeterminacy). In other words, $8\Delta$ comes from an element of $\pi_{24}(\Sigma^{20}\mathrm{tmf}\wedge C\nu)\cong\pi_{4}(\mathrm{tmf}\wedge C\nu)$ . Under the canonical map $\mathrm{tmf}\wedge C\nu\to\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ , this element corresponds to $2b_{2}\in\pi_{4}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu)$ . Similarly, the element $\Delta\eta\in\pi_{24}(\mathrm{tmf})$ can be related to the element $\sigma_{1}\in\pi_{5}(\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu)$ . This is related to the approach taken in [Dev19] to show that the Ando-Hopkins-Rezk orientation $\mathrm{MString}\to\mathrm{tmf}$ from [AHR10] is surjective on homotopy.

#### Remark 4.6.

One can give explicit $q$ -expansions for each of the generators of $\mathrm{H}^{0}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes\ast})\cong\mathbf{Z}[b_{2},b_{4},b_{6},b_{8}]$ . The element $b_{2}$ is related to the weight $2$ Eisenstein series via the $q$ -expansion:

$$ b_{2}=1-24\sum_{n\geq 1}\sigma_{1}(n)q^{n},\ \text{where }\sigma_{1}(n)=\sum_{d\geq 1,d|n}d. $$

#### Remark 4.7.

The explicit characteristic power series for the Witten genus (in [HBJ92, Section 6.3], for instance) shows that the Witten genus of a spin $4k$ -manifold is a modular form if its first Pontryagin class vanishes. This restriction arises essentially because of the appearance of a weight $2$ Eisenstein series, which is not a modular form, in the characteristic power series. By Remark 4.6, the weight $2$ Eisenstein series is in fact a global section of $\mathrm{H}^{0}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes\ast})$ , and so one might expect to be able to refine the orientation $\mathrm{MU}\langle 6\rangle\to\mathrm{tmf}$ from [AHR10] to an orientation $\mathrm{MSU}\to\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . We will return to this question in forthcoming work; see also Remark 3.6.

The following application is due to Rezk.

#### Corollary 4.8.

The $\mathbf{E}_{{1}}$ -ring $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ admits the structure of a homotopy commutative ring.

#### Proof.

We know that $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ only has $\mathrm{tmf}$ -module cells in dimensions divisible by $4$ , so all obstructions to its homotopy commutativity live in these dimensions. We know that these obstructions vanish after inverting $2$ , since $A[1/2]$ is homotopy commutative. By Theorem 4.1, all the homotopy groups of $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ in dimensions divisible by $4$ are torsion-free, so $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ must indeed be homotopy commutative. ∎

An immediate consequence of Theorem 3.7 and Corollary 4.8 is:

#### Corollary 4.9.

The stack ${M}_{\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu}$ associated to the homotopy commutative ring $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ is isomorphic to ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ .

#### Remark 4.10.

Corollary 4.9 implies, for instance, that the fact that $\nu$ is not detected by $L_{K(1)}\mathrm{tmf}$ is related to the existence of a dotted map

$$ \textstyle{{M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{ord}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{M}_{\mathrm{ell}},} $$

where ${M}_{\mathrm{ell}}^{\mathrm{ord}}$ denotes the moduli stack of ordinary elliptic curves. This existence of this dotted map is well-known in arithmetic geometry: it is the statement that the Frobenius (which exists for ordinary elliptic curves via quotienting out by the canonical subgroup) splits the Hodge filtration (see [Kat73, Section A2.3]).

Finally, we give the proof of Theorem 4.1.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We shall implicitly $2$ -localize everywhere; this is sufficient by Remark 4.4. We begin by calculating $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}({M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}};g^{\ast}\omega^{\otimes\ast})=\Ext_{\Sigma}(D,D)$ , where $(D,\Sigma)$ is the Hopf algebroid $(\mathbf{Z}[a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4},a_{6}],D[s,t])$ . Following [Sil86, Chapter III], define quantities

$$ b_{2}=a_{1}^{2}+4a_{2},\ b_{4}=2a_{4}+a_{1}a_{3},\ b_{6}=a_{3}^{2}+4a_{6},\ b_{8}=a_{1}^{2}a_{6}+4a_{2}a_{6}-a_{1}a_{3}a_{4}+a_{2}a_{3}^{2}-a_{4}^{2}. $$

Notice that $b_{2}b_{6}-b_{4}^{2}=4b_{8}$ and that $1728\Delta=c_{4}^{2}-c_{6}^{2}$ where $c_{4}$ , $c_{6}$ , and $\Delta$ are as in the theorem statement.

Let $I$ denote the ideal $(2,a_{1},a_{3},a_{4})$ , and define a Hopf algebroid

$$ (\overline{D},\overline{\Sigma})=(D/I,\Sigma/I)=(\mathbf{F}_{2}[a_{2},a_{6}],\overline{D}[s,t]). $$

The right unit sends

$$ a_{2}\mapsto a_{2}+s^{2},\ a_{6}\mapsto a_{6}+t^{2}. $$

Then there is a Bockstein spectral sequence

$$ E_{1}^{p,q,n}=\Ext^{p,n}_{\overline{\Sigma}}(\overline{D},\Sym^{q}_{\overline{D}}(I/I^{2}))\Rightarrow\Ext^{p,n}_{\Sigma}(D,D), $$

with $d_{r}:E_{r}^{p,q,n}\to E_{r}^{p+1,q+r,n}$ . Now, $I/I^{2}=\overline{D}\otimes_{\mathbf{F}_{2}}V$ , with $V=\mathbf{F}_{2}\{\overline{a}_{0},\overline{a}_{1},\overline{a}_{3},\overline{a}_{4}\}$ where $\overline{a}_{0}$ , $\overline{a}_{1}$ , $\overline{a}_{3}$ , and $\overline{a}_{4}$ represent $2$ , $a_{1}$ , $a_{3}$ , and $a_{4}$ respectively. The comodule structure $I/I^{2}\to I/I^{2}\otimes_{\overline{D}}\overline{\Sigma}$ sends

$$ \overline{a}_{0}\mapsto\overline{a}_{0},\ \overline{a}_{1}\mapsto\overline{a}_{1}+\overline{a}_{0}s,\ \overline{a}_{3}\mapsto\overline{a}_{3}+\overline{a}_{0}t,\ \overline{a}_{4}\mapsto\overline{a}_{4}+\overline{a}_{3}s+\overline{a}_{1}t+\overline{a}_{0}st. $$

There is a map $\overline{D}\to\mathbf{F}_{2}$ induced by sending $a_{2}$ and $a_{6}$ to zero, and so we obtain a Hopf algebroid $(\mathbf{F}_{2},C)$ with

$$ C=\mathbf{F}_{2}\otimes_{\overline{D}}\overline{\Sigma}\otimes_{\overline{D}}\mathbf{F}_{2}\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[a_{2},a_{6},s,t]/(a_{2},a_{6},\eta_{R}(a_{2}),\eta_{R}(a_{6}))\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[s,t]/(s^{2},t^{2})=E(s,t). $$

To emphasize the connection to homotopy theory, we write $h_{1}$ for $s$ and $h_{21}$ for $t$ . Now, the map $\overline{D}\to\mathbf{F}_{2}\otimes_{\overline{D}}\overline{\Sigma}=\mathbf{F}_{2}[h_{1},h_{21}]$ given by sending $a_{2}$ to $h_{1}^{2}$ and $a_{6}$ to $h_{21}^{2}$ is faithfully flat, and defines an isomorphism $(\overline{D},\overline{\Sigma})\to(\mathbf{F}_{2},C)$ of Hopf algebroids. Moreover, the Hopf algebroid $(\mathbf{F}_{2},C)$ presents the (graded) stack $B\alpha_{2}\times B\alpha_{2}$ over $\spec(\mathbf{F}_{2})$ . It follows that

$$ \Ext^{p,n}_{\overline{\Sigma}}(\overline{D},\Sym^{q}_{\overline{D}}(I/I^{2}))\cong\Ext^{p,n}_{C}(\mathbf{F}_{2},\Sym^{q}_{\mathbf{F}_{2}}(V))=\mathrm{H}^{p,n}(B\alpha_{2}\times B\alpha_{2};\Sym^{q}(V)). $$

The comodule structure on $I/I^{2}$ appearing in Equation (8) is a representation of $\alpha_{2}\times\alpha_{2}$ on $V$ , and so:

$$ \Ext^{0,\ast}_{C}(\mathbf{F}_{2},\Sym^{\ast}_{\mathbf{F}_{2}}(V))=V^{\alpha_{2}\times\alpha_{2}}=\mathbf{F}_{2}[\overline{a}_{0},\overline{a}_{1}^{2},\overline{a}_{0}\overline{a}_{4}+\overline{a}_{1}\overline{a}_{3},\overline{a}_{3}^{2},\overline{a}_{4}^{2}]; $$

indeed, these are the invariants under the $\alpha_{2}\times\alpha_{2}$ -action on $V$ . Moreover, by looking at the expressions for $b_{2}$ , $b_{4}$ , $b_{6}$ , and $b_{8}$ , we find that they are represented by $\overline{a}_{1}^{2}$ , $\overline{a}_{0}\overline{a}_{4}+\overline{a}_{1}\overline{a}_{3}$ , $\overline{a}_{3}^{2}$ , and $\overline{a}_{4}^{2}$ , respectively; in particular, all of the generators of $V^{\alpha_{2}\times\alpha_{2}}$ are permanent cycles in the Bockstein spectral sequence. Moreover, $\mathrm{H}^{\ast,\ast}(B\alpha_{2}\times B\alpha_{2};\Sym^{q}(V))\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}$ for $q\geq 1$ , and for $q=0$ we have $\mathrm{H}^{\ast,\ast}(B\alpha_{2}\times B\alpha_{2};\Sym^{0}(V))\cong\mathbf{F}_{2}[h_{1},h_{21}]$ , where $h_{1}=[s]$ and $h_{21}=[t]$ . Together with Equation (9), we obtain a complete calculation of the $E_{1}$ -page of the Bockstein spectral sequence (7).

The right unit in Equation (5) gives Bockstein differentials $a_{1}\mapsto 2h_{1}$ and $a_{3}\mapsto 2h_{21}$ , which correspond to $2\eta$ and $2\sigma_{1}$ being null, respectively. Moreover,

$$ d(a_{4}^{2})=a_{3}^{2}s^{2}+a_{1}^{2}t^{2}+4s^{2}t^{2}+4a_{1}st^{2}-2a_{1}a_{3}st-4a_{3}s^{2}t $$

in the cobar complex, and

$$ s^{2}b_{6}+t^{2}b_{2}=a_{3}^{2}s^{2}+a_{1}^{2}t^{2}+4a_{6}s^{2}+4a_{2}t^{2}. $$

Since $a_{2}=0$ and $a_{6}=0$ , we have $a_{1}s=-s^{2}$ and $a_{3}t=-t^{2}$ . This produces a differential with target $h_{1}^{2}b_{6}+h_{21}^{2}b_{2}$ . Combining together all of these facts gives Equation (6) as the cohomology of the moduli stack ${M}_{\mathrm{cub}}^{\mathrm{dR}}$ . As in Corollary 3.8, this is the $E_{2}$ -page of the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . We now calculate the Adams–Novikov differentials. The $15$ -skeleton of $A$ is as shown in Figure 1.

We know that $\eta^{3}=4\nu$ vanishes in $\pi_{\ast}A$ , so $h_{1}^{3}$ must die in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . There is only one possibility, namely the $d_{3}$ -differential $d_{3}(b_{2})=h_{1}^{3}$ . (Note that this differential already exists in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $A$ , where $b_{2}$ is represented by $v_{1}^{2}$ , i.e., the class $[y_{2}]$ in the cobar complex (via Proposition 3.3).) As a consequence, both $\eta$ and $\sigma_{1}$ are permanent cycles in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $A$ .

Next, we know from Proposition 3.3 that $\sigma_{1}$ is detected in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $A$ by $h_{21}$ . Since $\sigma_{1}\in\langle\eta,\nu,1_{A}\rangle$ , one has that $\eta^{2}\sigma_{1}=0$ in $\pi_{\ast}A$ , so $h_{1}^{2}h_{12}$ must die in $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . There is no possibility other than $d_{3}(b_{4})$ for a differential to kill $h_{1}^{2}h_{21}$ (except for a $d_{3}$ -differential on $b_{2}^{2}$ , but this cannot kill $h_{1}^{2}h_{12}$ ). Note that $h_{1}h_{12}$ is a permanent cycle and represents $\eta\sigma_{1}$ .

For the third differential, note that since $\sigma_{1}\in\langle\eta,\nu,1_{A}\rangle$ , we have $\eta\sigma_{1}^{2}=0$ . There is only one possibility, namely $d_{3}(b_{6})=h_{1}h_{21}^{2}$ . (Since there is a $d_{3}$ -differential $d_{3}(b_{2})=h_{1}^{3}$ , we have $d_{3}(h_{21}^{2}b_{2})=h_{1}^{3}h_{21}^{2}$ . But there is a relation $h_{1}^{2}b_{6}=h_{21}^{2}b_{2}$ , so $d_{3}(h_{1}^{2}b_{6})=h_{1}^{3}h_{21}^{2}$ , which also forces $d_{3}(b_{6})=h_{1}h_{21}^{2}$ .) Note that $h_{12}^{2}$ is a permanent cycle and represents $\sigma_{1}^{2}$ .

Finally, $\sigma_{1}^{3}=0$ in $\pi_{\ast}A$ (and therefore in $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ ). It follows that the element $h_{21}^{3}$ must be the target of a differential in the Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ . The only possibilities are a $d_{3}$ -differential on $b_{4}^{2}$ , $b_{2}b_{6}$ , or $b_{8}$ . Only $b_{8}$ can kill $h_{21}^{3}$ , and we conclude the $d_{3}$ -differential $d_{3}(b_{8})=h_{21}^{3}$ . At this point, there are no more possibilities for differentials in the descent/Adams–Novikov spectral sequence for $\mathrm{tmf}/\!\!/\nu$ , and the spectral sequence collapses at the $E_{4}$ -page.

# On the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings, & the metastable EHP sequence

**Authors:** Sanath Devalapurkar and Peter Haine

## Abstract

This note provides modern proofs of some classical results in algebraic topology, such as the James Splitting, the Hilton–Milnor Splitting, and the metastable EHP sequence. We prove fundamental splitting results

in the maximal generality of an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts in which pushouts squares remain pushouts after basechange along an arbitrary morphism (i.e., Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds). For connected objects, these imply the classical James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings. Moreover, working in this generality shows that the James and Hilton–Milnor splittings hold in many new contexts, for example in: elementary $\infty$ -topoi, profinite spaces, and motivic spaces over arbitrary base schemes. The splitting results in this last context extend Wickelgren and Williams’ splitting result for motivic spaces over a perfect field. We also give two proofs of the metastable EHP sequence in the setting of $\infty$ -topoi: the first is a new, non-computational proof that only utilizes basic connectedness estimates involving the James filtration and the Blakers–Massey Theorem, while the second reduces to the classical computational proof.

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction 1.1 Linear overview 1.2 Notation & background

- 2 The James Splitting 2.1 Universal pushouts and Mather’s Second Cube Lemma 2.2 Statement of the James Splitting & Consequences 2.3 Proof of the James Splitting 2.4 Ganea’s Lemma

- 3 The Hilton–Milnor Splitting 3.1 Reminder on group objects & the Splitting Lemma

- 4 Connectedness & the James Splitting 4.1 Connectedness and the Blakers–Massey Theorem 4.2 The infinite James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings

- 5 The James filtration & metastable EHP sequence 5.1 The James filtration 5.2 Splitting the James filtration 5.3 Proofs of the metastable EHP sequence

- References

## 1. Introduction

A classical result of James shows that given a pointed connected space $X$ , the homotopy type $\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ given by suspending the loopspace on the suspension of $X$ splits as a wedge sum

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i} $$

of suspensions of smash powers of $X$ [55, 67]. Hilton and Milnor proved a related splitting result [63, 64, 72]: given pointed connected spaces $X$ and $Y$ , they showed that there is a homotopy equivalence

$$ \Omega\Sigma(X\vee Y)\simeq\Omega\Sigma X\times\Omega\Sigma Y\times\Omega\Sigma\left(\bigvee_{i,j\geq 1}X^{\wedge i}\wedge Y^{\wedge j}\right)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In the classical setting, these splitting results follow from combining a connectedness argument using the hypothesis that $X$ and $Y$ are connected with the following more fundamental splittings: given any pointed spaces $X$ and $Y$ , there are natural equivalences

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\Sigma X\vee(X\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\text{\qquad and\qquad}\Omega(X\vee Y)\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The first objective of this note is to provide clear, modern, and non-computational proofs of these fundamental splittings (1.3). The only property particular to the $\infty$ -category of spaces that our proofs utilize is Mather’s Second Cube Lemma [70]; this asserts that pushout squares remain pushouts after basechange along an arbitrary morphism (see §​ 2.1). Hence these ‘fundamental’ James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings hold in any $\infty$ -category where we can make sense of suspensions, loops, wedge sums, and smash products, and have access to Mather’s Second Cube Lemma:

#### Theorem 1.4 (Fundamental James Splitting; Theorem 2.10).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts, and assume that Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in $\mathcal{X}$ . Then for every pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma X\vee(X\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} n\geq 1 \displaystyle\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X \displaystyle\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In general, the infinite splitting $\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}$ need not hold; roughly speaking, the problem is that if $X$ is not connected, then $(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)$ need not vanish as $n\to\infty$ . However, there is always a natural map $\bigvee_{i\geq 1}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ .

#### Theorem 1.5 (Fundamental Hilton–Milnor Splitting; Theorem 3.1).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts, and assume that Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in $\mathcal{X}$ . Then for every pair of pointed objects $X,Y\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ there is an natural equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Omega(X\vee Y) \displaystyle\simeq\Omega X\times\Omega Y\times\Omega\Sigma(\Omega X\wedge\Omega Y)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

In §​ 4.2 we explain in what generality the the infinite James Splitting (1.1) and Hilton–Milnor Splitting (1.2) hold, and how to deduce them from Theorems 1.4 and 1.5.

It might seem that knowing that the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings in this level of generality is of dubious advantage; the settings in which one is most likely to want to apply these splittings are the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{Spc}$ of spaces (where the results are already known), or an $\infty$ -topos (where the results follows immediately from the results for $\mathbf{Spc}$ ; see §​ 4.2). However, algebraic geometry provides an example that does not immediately follow from the result for spaces: motivic spaces. The obstruction is that the $\infty$ -category of motivic spaces over a scheme is not an $\infty$ -topos; since motivic localization almost never commutes with taking loops, knowing the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings in the $\infty$ -topos of Nisnevich sheaves does not allow one to deduce that they hold in motivic spaces.

Wickelgren and Williams used the James filtration to prove that the infinite James Splitting (1.1) holds for $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connected motivic spaces over a perfect field [85, Theorem 1.5]. The reason for the restriction on the base is because their proof relies on Morel’s unstable $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connectivity Theorem [73, Theorems 5.46 and 6.1], which implies that motivic localization commutes with loops [51, 73]. However, the unstable $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connectivity property does not hold for higher-dimensional bases [51, 52], so a different method is needed if one wants to prove James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings for motivic spaces over more general bases. This is where our generalization pays off: work of Hoyois [66, Proposition 3.15] shows that, in particular, Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in motivic spaces over an arbitrary base scheme. Therefore, Theorems 1.4 and 1.5 apply in this setting. We use these splittings to give a description of the motivic space $\Sigma\Omega\mathbf{P}^{1}$ in terms of wedges of motivic spheres $\mathrm{S}^{i+1,i}$ (Example 2.14), and also give a new description of $\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ (Example 3.3). Over a perfect field, we give a new decomposition of $\Omega\Sigma^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ in terms of motivic spheres of the form $\mathrm{S}^{2m+1,m}$ (Example 4.25).

The second goal of this note is to give a modern construction of the metastable EHP sequence in an $\infty$ -topos $\mathcal{X}$ . For every pointed connected object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , the James Splitting provides Hopf maps

$$ h_{n}\colon\Omega\Sigma X\to\Omega\Sigma(X^{\wedge n})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

There is also a James filtration $\{\mathrm{J}_{m}(X)\}_{m\geq 0}$ on $\Omega\Sigma X$ , and, moreover, the composite

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega\Sigma X^{\wedge n}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h_{n}} $$

is trivial. The sequence (1.6) is not a fiber sequence in general11 1 When $\mathcal{X}$ is the $\infty$ -category of spaces and $X$ is a sphere, James and Toda proved that, roughly, the sequence (1.6) becomes a fiber sequence after $p$ -localization. See [68, 69, 83]for a precise statement., but is in the metastable range:

#### Theorem 1.7 (metastable EHP sequence; Theorem 5.19).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -topos, $k\geq 0$ an integer, and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed $k$ -connected object. Then for each integer $n\geq 1$ , the morphism $\mathrm{J}_{n-1}(X)\to\textup{fib}(h_{n})$ is $((n+1)(k+1)-3)$ -connected.

We note here that a morphism is $m$ -connected in our terminology if and only if it is $(m+1)$ -connected in the classical terminology (see Warning 4.9).

We provide two proofs of Theorem 1.7. The first proof is new and non-computational; it only makes use of some basic connectedness estimates involving the James filtration and the Blakers–Massey Theorem. In the second proof we simply note that Theorem 1.7 for a general $\infty$ -topos follows immediately from the claim for the $\infty$ -topos of spaces. In the case of spaces, we provide a computational proof; we include this second proof because we were unable to find the computational proof we were familiar with in the literature.

### 1.1. Linear overview

We have written this note with two audiences in mind: the student interested in seeing proofs of Theorems 1.4, 1.5 and 1.7 in the classical setting of spaces, and the expert homotopy theorist interested in applying these results to more general contexts such as motivic spaces or profinite spaces. The student can always take $\mathcal{X}$ to be the $\infty$ -category of spaces, and the expert can safely skip the background sections provided for the student. We also note that this text should still be accessible to the reader familiar with homotopy (co)limits but unfamiliar with higher categories, since all we use in our proofs are basic manipulations of homotopy (co)limits.

Section 2 is dedicated to proving Theorem 1.4. In §​ 2.1, we provide background on Mather’s Second Cube Lemma and the universality of pushouts. In §​ 2.2, we provide a proof of the James Splitting. Our proof is roughly the same as proofs presented elsewhere [65, 82, 86], but it seems that the generality of the argument we present here is not very well-known.

Section 3 provides a quick proof of Theorem 1.5. Again, shadows of the proof we provide appear in the literature [59, 60, 82], but it seems that the generality of the proof has not been completely internalized by the community. As an application, we use work of Wickelgren [84, Corollary 3.2] to give a new description of the motivic space $\Omega\Sigma(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ (Example 3.2).

Section 4 explains how to use a connectedness argument to prove the infinite James Splitting (1.1) and Hilton–Milnor Splitting (1.2) for pointed connected objects of an $\infty$ -topos, and for pointed $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -connected motivic spaces over a perfect field. In §​ 4.1, we begin by recalling the basics of connectedness and the Blakers–Massey Theorem in an $\infty$ -topos; this material is also instrumental in our proof of Theorem 1.7. Subsection 4.2 presents the connectedness argument needed to deduce the infinite splittings and defines the Hopf maps appearing in Theorem 1.7. As an application we give a new description of the motivic space $\Omega\Sigma^{2}(\mathbf{P}^{1}\smallsetminus\{0,1,\infty\})$ over a perfect field (Example 4.25).

Section 5 is dedicated to proving Theorem 1.7. In §​ 5.1, we provide the background on the James filtration needed to understand the statement of Theorem 1.7, as well as some connectedness estimates we need to prove Theorem 1.7. In §​ 5.2, we give a refinement of the James Splitting in terms of the James filtration. In §​ 5.3, we first provide a proof of Theorem 1.7 using the Blakers–Massey Theorem (which we have not seen elsewhere), and then record for posterity what we imagine is the standard computational proof of Theorem 1.7.

## 2. The James Splitting

In this section, we present a proof of the James Splitting which holds in any $\infty$ -category with finite limits and pushouts, where pushout squares remain pushouts after basechange along an arbitrary morphism. The argument we give roughly follows the argument Hopkins gave in his course on stable homotopy theory in the setting of spaces [65, Lecture 4, §3]; Hopkins attributes this proof to James [67, 68, 69]and Ganea [58].

### 2.1. Universal pushouts and Mather’s Second Cube Lemma

The key property utilized in the proofs we present of the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings is that pushout squares are preserved by arbitrary basechange. This implies that, in particular, the James and Hilton–Milnor Splittings hold in any $\infty$ -topos, but also in other situations (such as motivic spaces). In this subsection, we provide the categorical context that we work in for the rest of the paper and give a convenient reformulation of the stability of pullbacks under basechange in terms of Mather’s Second Cube Lemma (Lemma 2.6).

#### Recollection 2.1.

Let $\mathcal{I}$ be an $\infty$ -category and let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pullbacks and all $\mathcal{I}$ -shaped colimits. We say that $\mathcal{I}$ -shaped colimits in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal if $\mathcal{I}$ -shaped colimits in $\mathcal{X}$ are stable under pullback along any morphism. That is, for every diagram $F\colon\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{X}$ and pair of morphisms $\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{i\smallin\mathcal{I}}F(i)\to Z$ and $Y\to Z$ in $\mathcal{X}$ , the natural morphism

$$ \operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{i\smallin\mathcal{I}}(F(i)\times_{Z}Y)\to\Big(\operatornamewithlimits{colim}_{i\smallin\mathcal{I}}F(i)\Big)\times_{Z}Y $$

is an equivalence.

#### Example 2.2.

Let $0\leq n\leq\infty$ , and let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $n$ -topos. One of the Giraud–Lurie axioms for $n$ -topoi guarentees that all small colimits in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal [44, Theorem 6.1.0.6 & Proposition 6.4.1.5]. In particular, small colimits in the category $\mathbf{Set}$ of sets and the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{Spc}$ of spaces are universal.

#### Example 2.3.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an elementary $\infty$ -topos in the sense of [77, Definition 3.5]. Then all colimits that exist in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal [77, Corollary 3.12]. In particular, finite colimits are universal in $\mathcal{X}$ .

#### Example 2.4 (motivic spaces).

Let $S$ be a scheme. The $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ of motivic spaces over $S$ is defined as the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -localization of the $\infty$ -topos $\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})$ of sheaves of spaces on the category $\mathbf{Sm}_{S}$ of smooth schemes of finite type over $S$ equipped with the Nisnevich topology. Concretely, $\mathbf{H}(S)$ is the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})$ spanned by those Nisnevich sheaves $\mathcal{F}$ on $\mathbf{Sm}_{S}$ with the property that for each smooth $S$ -scheme $X$ , the projection $\pr_{1}\colon X\times_{S}\mathbf{A}_{S}^{1}\to X$ induces an equivalence

$$ \pr_{1}^{{\mathbin{*}}}\colon\mathcal{F}(X)\similarrightarrow\mathcal{F}(X\times_{S}\mathbf{A}_{S}^{1})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

The inclusion $\mathbf{H}(S)\subset\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})$ admits a left adjoint $\Lmot\colon\operatorname{Sh}_{\Nis}(\mathbf{Sm}_{S})\to\mathbf{H}(S)$ called motivic localization. Motivic localization preserves finite products, but not all finite limits. Moreover, the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ is not an $\infty$ -topos (see [81, 76]), and it is not immediately clear from the construction if any colimits are universal in $\mathbf{H}(S)$ . Nonetheless, Hoyois has shown that all small colimits are universal in $\mathbf{H}(S)$ [66, Proposition 3.15].

#### Example 2.5 (profinite spaces).

We say that a space $X$ is $\mathrm{\pi}$ -finite if $X$ is truncated, has finitely many connected components, and $\mathrm{\pi}_{i}(X,x)$ is finite for every integer $i\geq 1$ and point $x\smallin X$ . Write $\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}}\subset\mathbf{Spc}$ for the full subcategory spanned by the $\mathrm{\pi}$ -finite spaces and $\Pro(\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}})$ for the $\infty$ -category of profinite spaces. Infinite coproducts in $\Pro(\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}})$ are not universal [46, Warning E.6.0.9], however, finite colimits and geometric realizations of simplicial objects are universal in $\Pro(\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{\pi}})$ [46, Theorem E.6.3.1 & Corollary E.6.3.2].

The following result gives a reformulation of what it means for pushouts to be universal in terms of Mather’s Second Cube Lemma, which Mather originally proved in the $\infty$ -category of spaces [70, Theorem 25]. See [47, Tag 011H] for an elegant proof of Mather’s Second Cube Lemma in $\mathbf{Spc}$ .

#### Lemma 2.6.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with pullbacks and pushouts. The following conditions are equivalent:

- (2.6.1) Pushouts in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal.

- (2.6.2) Mather’s Second Cube Lemma holds in $\mathcal{X}$ : Given a commutative cube ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{3}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{0}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}}$ ${\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{3}}$ in $\mathcal{X}$ where the bottom horizontal face is a pushout square and all vertical faces are pullback squares, then the top horizontal square is a pushout square.

#### Proof.

The implication (2.6.1) $\Rightarrow$ (2.6.2) is immediate. To see that (2.6.2) $\Rightarrow$ (2.6.1), suppose that we are given a pushout square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{3}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\ulcorner} $$

in $\mathcal{X}$ and morphisms $f\colon B_{3}\to Z$ and $g\colon Y\to Z$ in $\mathcal{X}$ . For each $i\smallin\{0,1,2,3\}$ , define $A_{i}\coloneq B_{i}\times_{Z}Y$ , so that all the vertical squares in the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A_{3}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{2}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B_{3}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f} $$

Since the main results of this note are about pointed objects, we make the following mildly abusive convention:

#### Convention 2.9.

We say that an $\infty$ -category $\mathcal{X}$ has universal pushouts if $\mathcal{X}$ has finite limits and pushouts, and pushouts in $\mathcal{X}$ are universal.

### 2.2. Statement of the James Splitting & Consequences

The James Splitting, originally proven in [67], provides a splitting of the space $\Omega\Sigma X$ after a single suspension. The goal of this subsection is to provide a proof of the James Splitting that only relies on the universality of pushouts and a few elementary computations involving the interaction between forming suspensions, loop objects, and smash products.

#### Theorem 2.10 (Fundamental James Splitting).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts. For every pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\Sigma X\vee\Sigma(X\wedge\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Using the fact that $\Sigma(X\wedge\Omega\Sigma X)\simeq X\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ (Lemma 2.26) and iterating the equivalence of Theorem 2.10, we see:

#### Corollary 2.11 (Fundamental James Splitting, redux).

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts. For each pointed object $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ and integer $n\geq 1$ , there is a natural equivalence

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

#### Notation 2.12.

Let $\mathcal{X}$ be an $\infty$ -category with universal pushouts and $X\smallin\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ a pointed object. Assume that $\mathcal{X}_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ has countable coproducts. Passing to the colimit as $n\to\infty$ , the coproduct insertions

$$ \bigvee_{i=1}^{n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X $$

provided by Corollary 2.11 provide a natural comparison morphism

$$ \bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\hbox to0.0pt{\ ,\hss} $$

which we denote by $c_{X}\colon\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X$ .

#### Warning 2.13.

The comparison morphism $c_{X}$ need not be an equivalence. For example, if $\mathcal{X}=\mathbf{Spc}$ and $X=\mathrm{S}^{0}$ is the $0$ -sphere, then the map

$$ c_{\mathrm{S}^{0}}\colon\bigvee_{i=1}^{\infty}\mathrm{S}^{1}\to\Sigma\Omega\Sigma\mathrm{S}^{0}\simeq\bigvee_{i\smallin\mathbf{Z}}\mathrm{S}^{1} $$

is not an equivalence. Even though both the source and target of $c_{\mathrm{S}^{0}}$ are both countable wedges of copies of $\mathrm{S}^{1}$ , the map $c_{\mathrm{S}^{0}}$ is the summand inclusion induced by the inclusion $\mathbf{Z}_{\geq 1}\subset\mathbf{Z}$ .

We analyze when the comparison morphism $c_{X}$ is an equivalence in §​ 4.2.

#### Example 2.14.

Let $S$ be a scheme. Since colimits are universal in the $\infty$ -category $\mathbf{H}(S)$ of motivic spaces over $S$ (Example 2.4), Theorem 2.10 implies that for any pointed motivic space $X\smallin\mathbf{H}(S)_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ and integer $n\geq 1$ , we have $\mathrm{S}^{1}$ -James Splittings

$$ \Sigma\Omega\Sigma X\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma X^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(X^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\Sigma X)\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Write $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ for the multiplicative group scheme over $S$ . Since $\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}\simeq\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}$ , setting $X=\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ we see that

$$ \Sigma\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\Sigma\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}^{\wedge i}\right)\vee(\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}^{\wedge n}\wedge\Sigma\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

Using the grading convention $\mathrm{S}^{a,b}\coloneq\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}^{\wedge b}\wedge(\mathrm{S}^{1})^{\wedge(a-b)}$ for motivic spheres, we can rewrite the equivalence (2.15) as

$$ \Sigma\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1}\simeq\left(\bigvee_{1\leq i\leq n}\mathrm{S}^{i+1,i}\right)\vee(\mathrm{S}^{n+1,n}\wedge\Omega\mathbf{P}_{S}^{1})\hbox to0.0pt{\ .\hss} $$

#### Remark 2.16.

There is another suspension in motivic homotopy theory, given by smashing with the multiplicative group scheme $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ . One would like an analogue of the James Splitting in $\mathbf{H}(S)_{{\mathbin{*}}}$ for $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ -suspensions. For $S=\spec(\mathbf{R})$ , Betti realization defines a functor $\mathbf{H}(\spec(\mathbf{R}))\to\mathbf{Spc}_{\mathrm{C}_{2}}$ to $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -spaces which sends $\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}$ to the sign representation circle $\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{\sigma}}$ and $\mathrm{S}^{1}$ to the circle with trivial $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -action. Even though Betti realization is not an equivalence, it closely ties $\mathbf{R}$ -motivic homotopy theory with $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -equivariant homotopy theory. In [62], Hill studies the signed James construction in $\mathrm{C}_{2}$ -equivariant unstable homotopy theory, and shows that an analogue of the James Splitting holds for $\Omega^{\mathrm{\sigma}}\Sigma^{\mathrm{\sigma}}X$ after suspending by the regular representation sphere $\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{\rho}}=\mathrm{S}^{1}\wedge\mathrm{S}^{\mathrm{\sigma}}$ . This might lead one to hope that there is an analogue of Hill’s result in motivic homotopy theory which proves the James Splitting for $\Omega_{\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}}\Sigma_{\mathbf{G}_{\operatorname{m}}}X$ after $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ -suspension; at the moment, we are not aware of such a result.
